c: According to the sagas, the Northern Isles were Christianised by Olav Tryggvasson in 995 when he stopped at South Walls on his way from Ireland to Norway.

t: Niall Caille succeeds Conchobar
c: Conchobar was succeeded by Niall Caille in 833.

c: The Annals of the Four Masters connect him with attacks on Connacht, Mide and the church at Clonmacnoise in 844.

t: Viking fleet appears at Waterford Harbour
c: In 914 a new Viking fleet appeared in Waterford Harbour, and soon the Uí Ímair followed, again taking control over Viking activities in Ireland.

t: Niall Glúndub becomes Uí Néill overking
c: Niall Glúndub had followed Flann Sinna as Uí Néill overking in 916, and he marched into Munster against Ragnall, but no decisive engagement followed.

t: Ragnall becomes king of York
c: Ragnall left Ireland again in 918, and became king of York.

t: Gofraid attempts kingship of York
c: When Sihtric died in 927 Gofraid left for York, trying to assume kingship there.

t: Amlaíb defeats Limerick
c: He was succeeded by his son, Amlaíb, who inflicted a decisive defeat on Limerick in 937.

t: Amlaíb becomes king of York
c: Athelstan defeated this coalition at Brunanburh (937), but after Athelstan's death in 939 Amlaíb became king of York.

t: Muirchertach sacks Dublin
c: In 944 he sacked Dublin, now ruled by Blácaire mac Gofrith.

t: Brian claims kingship over Ireland
c: In 1000, Brian turned against Máel Sechnaill, and by 1002 he had forced Máel Sechnaill to submit to him, and now claimed kingship over the whole of Ireland.

t: Flaithbertach Ua Néill revolts against Brian
c: In 1012, Flaithbertach Ua Néill revolted against Brian, and the following year Máel Mórda of Leinster and Sigtrygg of Dublin did too.

t: Synod of Cashel convenes

t: Malachy establishes Mellifont Cistercian monastery

t: Malachy resigns as archbishop of Armagh
c: Malachy resigned as archbishop of Armagh in 1136, but was appointed native papal legate to Ireland by Innocent II in 1139.

t: Synod of Kells-Mellifont convened
c: The Synod of Kells-Mellifont was convened in 1152, with Paparo presiding as papal legate.

t: First Viking raids begin in Ireland
c: The First Viking Age in Ireland began in 795, when Vikings began carrying out hit-and-run raids on Gaelic Irish coastal settlements.

t: Irish kings drive Vikings from Dublin

t: Uí Ímair return to Ireland
c: However, in 914 the Vikings now known as the Uí Ímair (House of Ivar) would return to Ireland, marking the beginning of the Second Viking Age.

t: Vikings recorded on Lough Neagh
c: The first reference to the Vikings comes from the Annals of Ulster and the first entry for 841 AD reads: "Pagans still on Lough Neagh".

t: Vikings abduct King Máel Brigte
c: This has been identified with a raid on Conaille Muirthemne in 831 in which the king Máel Brigte was abducted by Vikings.

t: Viking fleet raids Dublin via River Liffey
c: In 837 a fleet of sixty longships sailed up the River Liffey and raided "churches, forts and dwellings", including presumably those at Dublin.

t: Vikings plunder Dún Masc and Irish settlements
c: In 845 the Vikings of Dublin plundered Dún Masc (Rock of Dunamase in County Laois), killing the abbot of Tír dá Glas (Terryglass in County Tipperary) and other…

t: Cerball defeats Vikings of Dublin at Carn Brammit
c: In 847 Cerball mac Dúnlainge the King of Osraige defeated the Norsemen of Dublin and their leader Agnonn (Hákon) at Carn Brammit.

t: Máel Sechnaill attempts peace with Amlaíb
c: According to the Fragmentary Annals of Ireland, Máel Sechnaill tried to come to terms with this dangerous new rival in 854, but without success.

t: Amlaíb returns to Dublin with brothers Ímar and Auisle
c: When Amlaíb returned to Dublin in 856 or 857, he was accompanied by two of his brothers, Ímar (Old Norse: Ívarr) and Auisle (Old Norse: Ásl).

t: Great Heathen Army arrives in England
c: The 10th-century historian Æthelweard noted that the fleet of the Great Heathen Army arrived "from the north" in 865 and wintered in East Anglia.

t: Hálfdan leads Great Heathen Army in England

t: Repton taken, fall of eastern Mercia
c: Repton was taken in 873, which led to the fall of eastern Mercia.

t: Halfdene divides Northumbria into two kingdoms

t: Hálfdan kills Eysteinn, takes Dublin
c: In 875 Albdann (Hálfdan) is reported to have "deceitfully killed" Amlaíb's son Oistín (Eysteinn) and taken Dublin.

t: Amlaíb and Ímar capture Dumbarton after siege

t: Viking kings massacre men in Ireland

t: Hálfdan slain at Loch Cuan
c: Hálfdan was slain in a battle with the Findgaill in Loch Cuan (Strangford Lough) in 877.

t: Oratory of St Cianán sacked at Duleek
c: Finally, in 881, he sacked the oratory of St Cianán at Damhliag in Brega (Duleek in Meath).

t: Barith dies, Mac Auisle succeeds him
c: Barith died in 881 shortly after sacking the oratory of St Cianán; he was succeeded by an unnamed son of Auisle, who is referred to in the annals as Mac Auisle.

t: Sichfrith routs High King Flann Sinna
c: In 888 Sichfrith routed the forces of the High King Flann Sinna (a son of Máel Sechnaill).

t: Sitric I assassinates Sichfrith Ivarsson
c: In 888 Sichfrith Ivarsson was assassinated by his brother Sitric I, who held the throne for five years.

t: Glúniarann leads raid on Armagh
c: In 895 a Norseman called Glúniarann ("Iron Knee", an Irish translation of the Norse Járnkné) led an army from Dublin to Armagh, where 710 prisoners were…

t: Kildare plundered by heathens
c:
Little is known of the reign of Ivar II; Kildare was plundered again by "the heathens" in 900, which may have been his doing.

t: Ivar II dies in Scotland
c:
Ivar II went to Scotland, where he died in 904.

Ímar ua Ímair; also known as Ivar II, was a Norse-Gaelic King of Dublin.

t: Olaf II defeats inhabitants of Saaremaa
c: About 1008, Olaf II Haraldsson, later king of Norway, landed on Saaremaa.

t: Battle between Estonian and Icelandic Vikings
c: A battle between Estonian and Icelandic Vikings off Saaremaa is described in Njál's saga as occurring in 972 AD.

t: Conrad of Franconia elected king of East Francia
c: Around 900, East Francia's autonomous stem duchies (Franconia, Bavaria, Swabia, Saxony, and Lotharingia) reemerged.

t: Holy Roman Empire dissolves during Napoleonic Wars
c: It developed in the Early Middle Ages (beginning in either 800 or 962), and lasted for a millennium until its dissolution in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars.

t: Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Roman Emperor
c: On 25 December 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne (the Frankish king) as Roman Emperor, reviving the title more than three centuries after the fall of the…

t: Empire renamed Holy Roman Empire of German Nation

t: Holy Roman Empire territories join German Confederation

t: Pepin becomes King of the Franks
c: In 751, Martel's son Pepin became King of the Franks, and later gained the sanction of the Pope.

t: Charlemagne becomes King of the Franks
c: In 768, Pepin's son Charlemagne became King of the Franks and began an extensive expansion of the realm.

t: Irene removes Constantine VI from throne
c: In 797, the Eastern Roman Emperor Constantine VI was removed from the throne by his mother, Empress Irene, who declared herself sole ruler.

t: Louis the Pious succeeds Charlemagne as emperor
c: After Charlemagne died in 814, the imperial crown passed to his son, Louis the Pious.

t: Carolingian rule ends with Charles the Fat's death
c: After the death of Charles the Fat in 888, Carolingian rule in the Roman Empire came to an end.

t: Death of Berengar I of Italy
c: The last such emperor was Berengar I of Italy, who died in 924.

t: Otto elected king in Aachen
c: Upon Henry the Fowler's death, Otto, his son and designated successor, was elected king in Aachen in 936.

t: Otto marries Adelaide of Italy
c: In 951, Otto came to the aid of Queen Adelaide of Italy, defeating her enemies, marrying her, and taking control over Italy.

t: Otto crowned emperor by Pope John XII
c: In 962, Otto was crowned emperor by Pope John XII, thus intertwining the affairs of the German kingdom with those of Italy and the Papacy.

t: Otto deposes Pope John XII
c: In 963, Otto deposed John XII and chose Leo VIII as the new pope (although John XII and Leo VIII both claimed the papacy until 964, when John XII died).

t: Otto III appoints Pope Gregory V
c: In 996 Otto III appointed his cousin Gregory V the first German pope.

t: Death of Otto III
c: Otto died young in 1002, and was succeeded by his cousin Henry II, who focused on Germany.

t: Conrad II elected king
c: Henry II died in 1024 and Conrad II, first of the Salian dynasty, was elected king only after some debate among dukes and nobles.

t: Lothair III elected emperor
c: When the Salian dynasty ended with Henry V's death in 1125, the princes chose not to elect the next of kin, but rather Lothair III, the moderately powerful but…

t: Conrad III elected Hohenstaufen emperor

t: Frederick Barbarossa crowned emperor
c: Frederick Barbarossa was crowned emperor in 1155.

t: Frederick Barbarossa dies during Third Crusade
c: In 1190, Frederick participated in the Third Crusade, dying in the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.

t: Teutonic Knights invited to Prussia
c: The Teutonic Knights were invited to Prussia by Duke Konrad of Masovia to Christianize the Prussians in 1226.

t: Murder of Philip of Swabia
c: After Philip was murdered in a private squabble in 1208, Otto prevailed for a while, until he began to also claim Sicily.

t: Frederick leads Sixth Crusade
c: Now, although excommunicated, Frederick led the Sixth Crusade in 1228, which ended in negotiations and a temporary restoration of the Kingdom of Jerusalem.

t: Imperial vassals gain legislative veto power
c: Even so, from 1232 the vassals of the emperor had a veto over imperial legislative decisions and any new law established by the emperor had to be approved by…

t: Bohemia raised to kingdom status

t: Death of Frederick II

t: Imperial crown contested between rivals

t: Rudolf I elected Holy Roman Emperor
c: After Richard's death in 1273, Rudolf I of Germany, a minor pro-Hohenstaufen count, was elected.

t: Death of Rudolf I
c: After Rudolf's death in 1291, Adolf and Albert were two further weak kings who were never crowned emperor.

t: Danish–Hanseatic War
c: This culminated in the Danish–Hanseatic War from 1361 to 1370.

t: Rudolf I grants Austria and Styria to sons
c: In 1282, Rudolf I thus lent Austria and Styria to his own sons.

t: Henry VII crowned Holy Roman Emperor
c: In 1312, Henry VII of the House of Luxembourg was crowned as the first Holy Roman Emperor since Frederick II.

t: Council of Constance resolves papal schism
c: The conflict between several papal claimants (two anti-popes and the "legitimate" Pope) ended only with the Council of Constance; after 1419 the Papacy…

t: Frederick III crowned first Habsburg Holy Roman Emperor
c: Frederick III was the first Habsburg to be crowned Holy Roman Emperor, in 1452.

t: Territorial princes lead Empire and Church reform
c: After 1440, the reform of the Empire and Church was sustained and led by local and regional powers, particularly the territorial princes.

t: Maximilian mediates between princes and Frederick
c: After Frederick retired to Linz in 1488, as a compromise, Maximilian acted as mediator between the princes and his father.

t: Reichshofrat established in Vienna
c: To create a rival for the Reichskammergericht, Maximilian established the Reichshofrat in 1497, which had its seat in Vienna.

t: Vehmic court abolished under Jérôme Bonaparte
c: The legal reform seriously weakened the ancient Vehmic court (Vehmgericht, or Secret Tribunal of Westphalia, traditionally held to be instituted by Charlemagne…

t: Perpetual Diet of Regensburg established
c: The Perpetual Diet of Regensburg was based in Regensburg from 1663 to 1806.

t: Berlin becomes capital of German Empire
c: A German capital in the true sense only existed in the Second German Empire from 1871, when the Kaiser, Reichstag and Reichskanzler resided in Berlin.

t: Habsburg conflicts cause merchant relocation
